subject: Chemistry
title: Prussian Blue: The First Modern Pigment
description: A quick win: understand Prussian Blue: The First Modern Pigment.

hook.text: Prussian blue was discovered by accident in 1706 when a paint maker used contaminated potash. It became the first modern pigment.

buildup.text: Heinrich Diesbach was making red pigment but his potash was tainted with animal blood. The result was deep blue.

discovery.text: The color comes from iron atoms in two oxidation states: Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺. Electrons jump between them, absorbing red light.

twist.text: Prussian blue is also a medical antidote. It traps radioactive cesium and thallium in the gut, preventing absorption.

climax.text: Blueprints were made with Prussian blue chemistry. The word 'blueprint' exists because of a paint accident.

punchline.text: Blood-contaminated potash, iron electrons jumping. An accident that colored the world.

quiz.question: What causes Prussian blue's intense color?
options: Electrons jumping between iron atoms in two different oxidation states
Cobalt molecules reflecting only blue wavelengths

details.summary: Prussian Blue, accidentally created by a Berlin dye maker in 1706, was the first synthetic pigment with a known chemical composition. Its intense blue color comes from charge transfer between iron atoms in two different oxidation states within its crystal lattice structure.
details.whyItMatters: Prussian Blue made affordable blue pigment available to artists for the first time, transforming European painting. It is now also used medically as an antidote for thallium and radioactive cesium poisoning.
takeaways: Charge transfer between iron oxidation states creates the blue color
It was the first blue pigment affordable enough for widespread art use
It treats thallium and radioactive cesium poisoning by trapping ions

faq.question: How can Prussian Blue be both a pigment and a medical treatment?
faq.answer: Prussian Blue's crystal lattice structure contains channels that trap metal ions through ion exchange. When taken orally for thallium or cesium poisoning, it binds these ions in the gut and prevents their absorption. The insoluble pigment passes through the body harmlessly.

faq.question: Why was Prussian Blue so revolutionary for European artists?
faq.answer: Before 1706, the only quality blue pigment was ultramarine ground from lapis lazuli, which cost more than gold. Prussian Blue was the first affordable, intense blue available to artists. It appears prominently in works by Hokusai, Gainsborough, and Picasso's Blue Period.
